title: On the Closed-Form of Flow Matching: Generalization Does Not Arise from Ta

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper first states and purports to prove the exact identity E[û*_M(x,t)] = û*(x,t) in Proposition 2(ii), calling the estimator unbiased. The following paragraph directly retracts this: “this does not guarantee unbiasedness in the standard Monte Carlo sense” and says that “the theoretical claims therefore approximate unbiasedness within empirical tolerance.” These statements are mutually incompatible. Either Eq. (10) is an exact theorem under the stated sampling scheme, or it is only approximate and requires explicit conditions/error bounds; both cannot be true.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.3, proof of Proposition 2(iii), Eqs. (70)–(74)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: There is a missing factor n in the variance proof. From Eq. (70), n/M E[sum_{j=1}^M w^(i_j)(u^(i_j))^2], with i_j uniform on n indices, equals sum_l w^(l)(u^(l))^2 = n E_{l~Unif}[w^(l)(u^(l))^2]. Eq. (71) instead drops the factor n and writes only E_{i_1~Unif}[w^(i_1)(u^(i_1))^2]. Consequently Eqs. (72)–(74) do not follow as written. The final intended inequality may be repairable, but the supplied proof is mathematically incorrect.

The velocity u is vector-valued in R^d, but the proof treats u^2 as a scalar and invokes convexity of x↦x^2. Likewise, the relation “Var[û*_M] ≤ Var[ucond]” is not defined for vector-valued random variables unless the authors specify a scalarization (for example trace/total variance) or the Loewner order on covariance matrices. The proposition and proof need a dimensionally valid variance definition and a corresponding proof.

Eq. (27) begins with a factor 1/n multiplying the sum, and Eq. (28) retains that factor. Eq. (29) drops 1/n without justification. The final closed-form ratio is unaffected because the same factor appears in the denominator, but Eq. (29), which is asserted to equal the numerator, is false as written.

The appendix says it presents “results for the MNIST dataset,” but both Table 1 and Table 2 are captioned “FID FMNIST.” The numerical trajectories strongly suggest the tables are for different datasets: Table 1 reaches FID 1.84 while Table 2 remains near 16.85, consistent with the accompanying mention of separate MNIST and FMNIST classifier accuracies. Thus at least one dataset label is wrong, and the paper does not reliably identify the provenance of the reported results.

The manuscript repeatedly makes causal and near-exclusive claims—e.g., “we rule out the noisy nature of the loss as a key factor,” “generalization ... emerges precisely when” the network fails to approximate û*, and Figure 2 “confirms that generalization arises when” this failure occurs. The reported evidence is observational across dataset sizes and architectures, with several changing quantities at once: the empirical target field itself, amount of training data, number of training epochs/exposures, and effective model/data complexity. The hybrid experiment establishes that replacing the early learned trajectory by the empirical field changes outputs, but it does not establish that approximation error, rather than architecture, optimization, or data geometry, is the cause of generalization. The paper itself later acknowledges these unaddressed factors, contradicting the strength of the earlier conclusions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Section 4.2, interpretation of EFM experiments
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The conclusion that target stochasticity is ruled out is stronger than the experiment supports. EFM with finite M is still a random minibatch estimator, and its target is not the exact closed-form field on the full training set. The paper reports only that performance did not significantly degrade in the tested configurations and explicitly admits that observed gains “remain within the expected noise range.” This supports, at most, no detected benefit of the particular target noise reductions tested; it cannot rule out a role for target stochasticity generally.

The central generation-dependent claims (Figures 2–4, FID, nearest-neighbor LPIPS, and hybrid trajectories) omit essential sampling protocol details: ODE solver, solver order, number of function evaluations or tolerances, time discretization, use of EMA versus raw parameters, generated sample counts for each metric, random seeds, and number of independent training runs. These choices materially affect flow-matching sample quality, memorization measurements, and hybrid trajectories. Listing only training hyperparameters is insufficient to reproduce or assess the reported comparisons.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph citing Kadkhodaie et al. (2024), Kamb and Ganguli (2025), and Ross et al. (2025)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text labels works as “Kadkhodaie et al. (2024, anticipated), Kamb and Ganguli (2025, manuscript), Ross et al. (2025, forthcoming).” In the paper's own references these are listed as published ICLR 2024, ICML 2025, and ICLR 2025 works, respectively. These bibliographic statuses are internally inconsistent and should be corrected.
